data.name: Bubbles
data.title: The classic bubble shooter, in your browser.
data.summary: Bubbles is an arcade bubble shooter you play in the browser or on your phone: line up a shot, match three or more and clear the board. It’s for anyone who wants a quick round that feels good on a small screen.
data.why: Quick to start, hard to put down. Bubbles has the depth of the arcade original — stars, scores and a global board — with modern controls, saved progress and music you can switch off. It runs in a browser tab, with nothing to install.
data.teaches: Closing an issue is a record of work. It is not proof that the product has finished the job.
data.site_og_description: A faithful, premium web-game re-implementation of a classic bubble shooter. Aim, match, and clear.

data.name: Fighter
data.title: Collect fighters. Build a squad. Pick your fight.
data.summary: Fighter is a collectible squad battler you play in the browser: collect characters, build a squad, then commit moves on a shared real-time Charge Strip. It’s for players who like turn-based combat with authored characters, story and several modes to work through.
data.why: Battles are quick and readable, and every fighter has their own look, voice and moves. There’s a collection to build and a story to follow, so a five-minute fight has somewhere to lead.
data.teaches: Prove one concrete variation before extracting a reusable product boundary. A product ambition is not a demonstrated white-label release.

data.name: SHOALSHOT
data.title: Read the tide. Place the shot.
data.summary: SHOALSHOT is a fishing game for phones and desktop: read the water, place your shot and land the catch. It’s for anyone who wants a calm, quick session, and it is designed phone-first.
data.why: Fishing games live or die on the feel of one cast, and this one keeps it simple: read the water, take the shot, see what you caught. It is designed phone-first, with a five-minute session in mind.
data.teaches: A release claim belongs to an exact build and a fresh observation. Old green evidence cannot qualify a newer head.

data.name: Protocol 11
data.title: A card game where the table changes every round.
data.summary: Protocol 11 is a card game for two to four players around one table, played solo or with friends. Twelve stages and a cast of characters make a house you play through, and every round brings a new Protocol.
data.why: Card games are better with company, and Protocol 11 plays two to four people at one table with no downloads. The round rules keep changing, so no two hands feel the same, and there’s a solo path through the twelve-stage House Circuit if you’d rather learn it alone.
data.teaches: A finished product needs play, visual judgement and exact release evidence to agree.

data.name: MAX
data.title: Your walker, made smarter.
data.summary: MAX is assistive technology for a wheeled walker: a companion app, a small computer on the walker and a gateway designed to find it, hear it and stop it. It’s for people who use a walker and the people who look after them.
data.why: When a walker goes missing in a care home or hospital, someone has to hunt for it. MAX aims to make finding it and stopping it a job for a phone, using the walker’s own hardware rather than another account to look after.
data.teaches: Software proof and physical proof are different kinds of evidence.
data.site_og_description: Keep your walker. Add Max. The connected companion prototype is being built around a simple FIND button, with voice and family support in development.

data.name: Pirates
data.title: Rebuilding a lost game from its own evidence.
data.summary: Pirates is a reconstruction of Master of the Secret Sea, built from the original game’s own source evidence rather than from memory. It’s for players who remember the original, and for anyone curious about how a lost game gets rebuilt honestly.
data.why: A reconstruction is only worth playing if it is the game that existed, rather than a guess wearing its name. Keeping what the source proves and saying plainly what it doesn’t is the difference between a rebuild and a tribute.
data.teaches: Sometimes the most intelligent agent action is to stop at the edge of the evidence.

data.name: LoftwahFM
data.title: Music, radio stations and original shows.
data.summary: LoftwahFM is a music catalogue, radio stations, original shows and a browser player that games can reuse. Listen to the stations and shows in your browser; game builders can drop the same player into their own game.
data.why: Music is most of what makes a game feel made, and LoftwahFM hands builders a catalogue, stations and a player they don’t have to build. Listeners get stations to leave running and original shows to replay.
data.teaches: A shared capability earns its name through compatible releases and real consumers. Published upstream code and verified game use are different evidence.

data.name: Social Club
data.title: Membership and hospitality, in prototype.
data.summary: Social Club is a membership and hospitality product: a working foundation for a private-club experience, from joining through to what members see.
data.why: A club is about how it feels to be a member, not just what the booking form does. The foundation works; that feeling is the standard the next design pass has to reach.
data.teaches: Product quality includes how a coherent interface feels as well as what its controls do.

data.name: Asset Hunter
data.title: A field guide to what can be made.
data.summary: Asset Hunter is a searchable catalogue of creative and technical assets that records where each one came from and what rights apply. It’s for builders and agents who need to know where something came from, what rights apply and who to credit.
data.why: Finding an asset is easy. Knowing where it came from, what rights apply and who to credit is the slow part. Asset Hunter records provenance and rights per item, and can package the permitted files into a reproducible archive you can hand on.
data.teaches: A deliverable is stronger evidence than a catalogue entry. Independent use is stronger evidence than a successful export.

data.site_og_description: A field guide to what can be made — distinct creative and technical possibilities across games, UI, branding, motion, audio, 3D, shaders, code and architecture, each with representative examples and their rights.

data.name: App Composer
data.title: Make software. Keep it yours.
data.summary: App Composer is a studio for building and maintaining web apps with a coding agent. Prepare the environment, shape the app and its editable content, then build a standalone application or reuse existing mini-apps. Loftwah’s Linkarooie creator page is a live example.
data.why: You bring the idea and keep the source in your own project. Get Ready handles supported setup, Init makes the brief concrete, and an agent builds the app around the content and features you need. EmDash provides editing and administration; your selected cloud account runs the result.
data.teaches: A checklist is not readiness. An exact HTTPS deployment and a verified change show that the build path works; another person completing setup is the next stronger proof.
data.site_og_title: Make software. Keep it yours. · App Composer
data.site_og_description: App Composer is an agent-operated studio for building applications with EmDash and Cloudflare. Get Ready prepares the environment, Init captures what the app should do, and independently maintained mini-apps connect through their data and actions.

children.text: This review puts eight projects on one dated page without pretending they share one definition of done. Some work is held by product quality, some by release evidence, some by source parity, and some by a real-world hardware trial.
Read each project on its own terms

Every project has its own dossier on this site. Each one states the reviewed state, the next useful proof and the boundary that state does not cross. A strong software result does not certify a finished product, and a past production observation does not establish that today's source is live.
Implementation, qualification, production verification and physical proof remain four separate records. Collapsing them is the most common way a portfolio report overstates a factory.
What the report keeps separate
Four boundaries run through every project in this factory, and each one has cost real work when it was blurred.
Implementation is not qualification. Code that exists and has been reviewed is a different record from code that has passed the checks required to be released.
A production claim belongs to the exact version observed. A deployment receipt names one Worker version and one review date; it does not speak for later source.
Software tests cannot prove how physical hardware behaves for a person in the world. That claim needs a physical trial and a dated observation.
Unknown source behaviour stays unknown until evidence resolves it. A reconstruction that cannot be read is recorded as ambiguous, not guessed.

content.quote: Progress is real when the work moves. Completion is real when the required evidence supports the claim.

children.text: The useful habit came before the agents.

The early stack was a reverse proxy, a VPS and WordPress plugins. I could join pieces that already did their jobs instead of rebuilding every capability. Composition was the skill: work out what each piece was good at, then make the pieces cooperate.

Plugins gave way to APIs, cloud services, infrastructure, models, skills and agents. The work moved from putting a website together towards operating the platform and its delivery. There was no clean line where a pair-programming tool became a factory. The coordination problem grew with the work.

children.text: Compose tools: use plugins, APIs and services for the jobs they already do well.
Work in a pair, then delegate: one human and one agent become bounded tasks with explicit owners.
Parallel work brings competing changes. Independent review and qualification become necessary.
Factory operation ties intent and work to evidence about an exact release. This is a sequence, not a dated timeline.
Writing code stopped being the only bottleneck.

As agents worked across several products for extended stretches, the coordination problem changed. With that much happening at once, I needed to know more than whether a task had started. What had changed? Who owned it? Had another agent challenged it? Had it reached the product anyone could actually open?

A backlog only helps if it can answer those questions. Bounded tasks and reviewable revisions make parallel work understandable. Durable records let the next agent pick it up without asking a human to remember every conversation.

“Done” was hiding several different questions.

data.title: The tests passed. The game still looked wrong.
data.deck: Fighter passed its geometry checks and still fell short of the product bar. The factory had measured whether the interface fitted. It had not measured whether the interface worked as a composition.
data.source_reference: Shareable factory snapshot reviewed 28 September 2026; no private repository or conversation material is reproduced.
data.lead: The interface did what the tests could see. The tests could not see what the player felt.
data.lesson: Geometry is evidence about geometry. Product judgement needs its own review.

children.text: The wrong question was easy to test.
The checks asked whether the interface fit its container and whether its geometry remained inside expected bounds. It did. The result still lacked hierarchy and compositional intent.
That was not a failure of the geometry checks. They answered the question they were built to answer. The mistake was treating their answer as a complete product judgement.

content.title: Initial belief
content.body: Responsive geometry and screenshot checks would prevent the important visual failures.

children.text: What the evidence could not see
A page can avoid clipping and still put the wrong thing first. A screen can be dimensionally correct while the player has to work to understand what matters, what changed or where to go next.

The factory therefore added three human checks: a visual review of the whole experience, a review of complete journeys and a copy check for generic or machine-written language. Reviewers identify the focal point, hierarchy, competing elements, context and quality of the complete experience.

content.quote: Geometry is evidence about geometry. It is not evidence that the product feels finished.

children.text: The lesson travelled

The same distinction later mattered in Bubbles: a technically valid interface was still challenged against its actual product bar. The factory’s lesson was not to discard automation. It was to stop asking one instrument to certify a different kind of quality.
What changed in the factory

Visual review became a named qualification stage. Whole journeys are reviewed with the implementation context in view. Responsive quality is judged at the states and orientations where people use the product. Passing a machine check is reported only as the claim that check supports.

data.title: A green build cannot find the real walker.
data.deck: MAX is a reminder that software qualification ends where physical use begins. The Pi, walker and person using FIND still have to meet in the real world.
data.source_reference: Shareable factory snapshot reviewed 28 September 2026; no private repository or conversation material is reproduced.
data.lead: A complete simulation is still a simulation.
data.lesson: Name the physical observation that remains. Do not borrow confidence from software tests.

children.text: Where the proof stops

MAX has a serious software foundation: pairing, a gateway, offline behaviour and remote FIND and STOP flows. Those capabilities matter. They do not put a Raspberry Pi next to the actual walker or show that a person can use its controls in their environment.

The physical path still needs the actual device, microphone, speaker, lights, network conditions and a real human interaction. A simulation, browser run or mocked response cannot replace that observation.
What remains unproven

The supplied factory report leaves real-walker FIND and the wider physical hardware path open. The public status keeps that limit visible instead of translating strong software maturity into a claim about a physical product.

data.title: Prove which build is live, or admit you do not know
data.deck: A public origin could not state which source it was serving. Rather than document that gap, this closes it: the build stamps its own fingerprint, the origin publishes it, and the deploy refuses to finish if the two disagree.
data.source_reference: The Woodhouse repository itself: the build-identity integration, the /build.json route, the shared verifier and the production deploy gate, reviewed 4 October 2026.
data.lead: A deploy receipt records what was intended to ship. For a long time nothing recorded what the public origin was actually serving, so those stayed two different claims.
data.lesson: A deployment that cannot report its own identity cannot be verified as current. Publishing the fingerprint is what turns "deployed" into "serving this exact build".

children.text: This was not a missing feature so much as a missing question. Every repository in this factory writes deploy notes, and several of them record a receipt naming a commit and a release. What none of them could do was ask the live origin what it was serving and get an answer. So a green deploy and a stale production could look identical from the outside, and the difference only surfaced later, as a bug report.

One product in this factory discovered the same gap from the other direction: it found production running behind its own default branch, with several hundred audit findings that were really just staleness. It had no way to name the live commit. That is the failure this work removes.
What the build stamps

A small build step computes a fingerprint over the exact source files that go into a deploy, alongside the commit that working tree sat on and whether that tree was clean. The value is substituted into the bundle at compile time, so nothing extra is written into the source tree and the deployed artefact carries no new file.

Reporting the tree's cleanliness matters more than it looks. A build made from a dirty tree corresponds to no reviewable commit at all, so a receipt naming a commit would be describing something that never existed as a unit.
What the origin refuses to claim

The endpoint does not report a Cloudflare Worker version identifier, because the runtime cannot know it. Only the deploy tool's output reveals it, and that value belongs in the private release receipt where it was observed rather than inferred.

That distinction is the whole point. An endpoint that could only approximate its own identity would eventually be quoted as though it were exact, and a number that is nearly right is worse than one that is honestly absent.
The gate is the useful half
Publishing an identity proves nothing on its own. The control that matters is the comparison.

Both deploy paths now read the live origin after deployment and refuse to continue unless the fingerprint it reports is the one that run just built. Preview is held to the same standard, because a preview that cannot prove its own source cannot support a production acceptance receipt.

The check was written once and shared. Standing alone it answers the question that is otherwise pure guesswork, which is what any given origin is serving right now. That matters most for products this factory does not own, where nobody has local access to compare against.

content.quote: A deployment that cannot report its own identity cannot be verified as current.

children.text: Reuse across the factory

The identity shape is deliberately small and published as a versioned schema, so a single verifier can check any product that adopts it. The products can keep their own judgement about what should ship; only the mechanism for proving what is live is meant to be shared.

This is the intended division: centralise the mechanism, keep the product judgement local. A shared media pipeline, a repository census or a resource lease earns the same treatment, but only once it has been shown to be genuinely the same problem in more than one place.

Adopting it is not retroactive. Nothing here claims another product publishes this yet, and no product is named as compliant. The capability exists, one product uses it, and the rest are free to ignore it until the question comes up.

data.title: Nine projects, and the first one you can check.
data.deck: Asset Hunter joins the portfolio as the first Woodhouse project whose repository and deployed commit anyone can verify. That changes what the other eight are allowed to imply.
data.source_reference: The public repository loftwah/asset-hunter and the public site assets.loftwah.com, reviewed 4 October 2026. Public commit identifiers and public issue titles are cited; no private repository body is reproduced.
data.lead: Eight projects on this site are summarised from a private readout. The ninth publishes the exact commit it was built from. That is not a small difference in confidence; it is a different kind of evidence.
data.lesson: A dated summary is evidence about a person. A pinned commit is evidence about a build. A portfolio needs both, and they are not interchangeable.

children.text: Asset Hunter is the ninth project on this site and the first one whose evidence anyone outside the factory can check. Its repository is public, its site publishes the commit it was built from, and its catalogue states its own size. Everything else here is an operator-reviewed summary of work the public cannot see.

The portfolio is reviewed project by project, not all at once, so this record now reports its newest review and says how many projects predate it. The eight launch projects still carry their 28 September 2026 date. Nothing about them was re-reviewed today, and nothing about them was changed.
What a public repository allows Woodhouse to claim

On 4 October 2026 the public Asset Hunter site reported commit 149836b4 as its build, and that commit was the head of its public main branch at the same moment. The two facts were read from the site and the repository rather than inferred from a deploy message, and a reader can repeat the check.

That is a stronger claim than any other project on this site can currently support. It establishes which source produced the page in front of you. It does not establish that the catalogue is complete, that any individual entry has cleared rights, or that the same commit will be live tomorrow. One observation of one origin on one day is what it is.
What a private readout cannot

The other eight projects are described from a shareable readout. Their states are accurate to the best of a dated human review, and this site will not pretend otherwise: the dossier for each one carries its own review date, its own source description and the boundary its state does not cross.

The asymmetry is worth stating plainly rather than smoothing over. A public repository lets a reader audit the record; a private one asks them to trust the operator. Both are legitimate records. Presenting the second as though it were the first would be the exact overstatement this publication exists to avoid.

content.quote: A dated summary is evidence about a person. A pinned commit is evidence about a build.

children.text: The work still open

Asset Hunter was public and moving on the review date, with 34 possibilities in the published catalogue and 53 issues plus one image-optimisation pull request open. The open work that matters is not feature count. It is rights correction and takedown, security and hostile-content review of a public catalogue, and production release evidence with a restore drill.
Until those exist, the catalogue is a growing public reference rather than a dependable one. Its dossier says so, and names those three as the next proofs.

data.title: Four projects solved four different problems.
data.deck: A portfolio review proposed extracting one shared agent-and-browser safety layer from the games and this site. Reading the actual implementations says the opposite: these are four specific failures with four earned answers, and a shared layer would have had to pick a side in each.
data.source_reference: A portfolio analysis supplied for this review date, checked against the private repositories and the deployed origins of Bubbles, SHOALSHOT, Fighter, Asset Hunter and Woodhouse on 5 October 2026. The recommendation is recorded because it was tested and did not survive; no private issue, pull request or conversation body is reproduced.
data.lead: The strongest claim in the review was that several projects had independently reinvented the same machinery and should stop. Reading the implementations, they had not reinvented anything. They had each hit a different failure.
data.lesson: Repetition of vocabulary is not repetition of semantics. Before extracting what looks like a shared layer, check whether the failures are the same failure.

children.text: The claim, stated fairly

A portfolio analysis of this factory concluded that the clearest hidden asset was not any individual game but the autonomous-engineering machinery the games kept rebuilding: agent contracts, browser contention, deterministic evidence, deployment verification, long-run reporting. It called that repetition the strongest signal in the factory, and recommended a narrowly scoped spike to extract the smallest shared layer and make three projects consume it.

That is a reasonable reading of a portfolio described from the outside. Four projects all run agents against browsers. Four projects all capture screenshots and gate on them. Four projects all verify deployments. The surface really does look like one capability wearing four uniforms.
What the implementations actually do
The proposal came with its own condition attached: verify first, and if the semantics are not the same, do not manufacture the abstraction. So we read them. Four capabilities, four different answers.

Browser contention. Bubbles inspects the process table, walks process ancestry, and refuses to start when another test lane is running — and it separates a person's interactive browser from an automation lane, because those are different claims about the host. SHOALSHOT takes a different shape entirely: an atomic lockfile with liveness reaping and a bounded wait, guarding a resource it owns. Same symptom, different blast radius, different mechanism, different failure mode if you get it wrong. Fighter does neither; it lets the operating system pick a port.

Visual evidence. Bubbles compares against checked-in images with a pixel-difference tolerance, because some of its frames are genuinely animated and a strict comparison would be permanently red. SHOALSHOT compares byte-for-byte, because it pins the clock and the locale and can therefore demand exactness. These are opposite engineering choices about what a passing comparison means. Bubbles risks letting a real change through; SHOALSHOT risks a false alarm. A shared helper would have had to choose, and each project chose against the other's failure.

Long-run reporting. Three projects, three different ideas of what an agent's report is allowed to rest on: an executable terminal proof checked against live repository state, a version-controlled ledger with claims and worktree health, and a written execution contract with a dated backlog census that openly admits its default-branch rules are procedural rather than enforced.

Deployment verification. Four mechanisms, no shared shape. This site publishes a named identity schema and fails a deploy that does not report the fingerprint it intended to ship. Asset Hunter carries its own commit in page metadata, answers a version endpoint, and ships a freshness gate that once wrongly declared a site stale seconds after it deployed. Fighter and SHOALSHOT each wrote their own release manifests. The one artefact genuinely shared across the factory is a doctrine document, referenced by name from more than one repository.
What survived
Two things, and neither is a framework.

The first is a pattern rather than a library: the projects learned the same lessons in the same order and recorded them. One project found that a screenshot tool's update mode rewrote only the baseline that had actually changed and reported everything green — and the fix for that became doctrine in another repository, cited by name. Cross-project learning happened in the reasoning, deliberately, with no code moving between repositories.

In the safety and release mechanisms inspected on 5 October 2026, no shared code dependency was found. Each mechanism answered a different failure. This dated finding does not rule out reuse in another subsystem; the 10 October music capability review records LoftwahFM separately.

content.quote: The shared asset is the argument, not the module.

children.text: What this site does with it

Nothing is being extracted. The honest outcome of the check is the outcome the recommendation allowed for: no shared primitive, and no justification for one. Manufacturing a framework here would have been the exact failure this publication exists to catch — an abstraction justified by the existence of complicated code rather than by a shared failure.

There is one concrete gap worth naming, and it is not about a shared layer. This site publishes a build-identity shape and describes it as intended for reuse across the factory. No other project in the factory has adopted it; each wrote its own. A published protocol with no adopters is a claim about intent, not about the fleet, and it should be described that way until something else actually uses it.
The part that was worth the exercise

The useful outcome is not an artefact. It is that a portfolio-level claim about this factory turned out to be checkable, and got checked. A recommendation arrived with a verification condition attached; the condition was honoured; the recommendation lost.

That is the whole method in one pass. A supplied analysis is a hypothesis with good reasoning behind it, not a fact to be republished. Where it matched the evidence we adopted it — including its most uncomfortable finding, which is that Asset Hunter's own backup drill reports that nobody has used it yet. Where it did not match, we recorded the disagreement rather than smoothing it over.

data.title: The empty tables are the answer.
data.deck: Asset Hunter's backup drill found that the tables holding a stranger's rating, rights report or dispute have never had a row. The useful part is not the zero. It is that the product found the zero, wrote it down, and refused to call the drill a pass.
data.source_reference: The public Asset Hunter repository and its production backup manifest, reviewed 5 October 2026. Counts are read from the project's own recorded backup; nothing is estimated.
data.lead: A catalogue grew to forty possibilities and learned to name the exact commit it was built from. In the same week, a backup recorded that nobody has rated it, reported it, disputed it, or asked for anything to be left uncrawled.
data.lesson: A negative measurement taken and published is worth more than a positive one inferred. The tables that would hold a user's judgement are empty, and the product says so in its own words rather than shipping around it.

children.text: What the backup says

The production backup taken on 4 October 2026 lists the tables it captured and how many rows each held. The administrator account and its passkey were there, one row each. The schema was there. Eighty-seven revisions were there. The catalogue was there, with forty examples and four curated collections.

The tables that exist so that somebody other than the author can act were empty. Ratings: zero. Rights reports: zero. Disputes: zero. Requests to exclude a source: zero. Moderation audit events: zero.
Why that is the most valuable thing in the project

This is the distinction the whole factory keeps trying to make, appearing for once as a number rather than as a principle. Building a discovery engine is implementation. Shipping it is release. Publishing the commit it was built from is production verification. None of those is demand.

Demand is a person rating something they found, reporting a rights problem they recognised, or disputing a judgement the catalogue made about them. Every mechanism for that exists and works. Not one person has used any of them.

A portfolio review supplied this week reached the same conclusion from the outside and called Asset Hunter the strongest standalone product candidate. Both readings are worth keeping. The product is the most complete thing in the factory. On demonstrated external use it is at zero, and it is the only project that can say so precisely.

content.quote: An empty table restoring as an empty table is not evidence that a row in it ever will.
content.attribution: Asset Hunter restore drill, reviewed 5 October 2026

children.text: The gate that refused to pass

The obvious response to a drill that finds empty tables is to make the drill green. This one does the opposite: it exits non-zero over exactly that condition, and says in its own documentation that a drill reporting green across untested tables is the failure it exists to prevent.

That is the behaviour worth copying. A verification step that cannot fail is decoration. This one can fail, it fails loudly for an honest reason, and the failure is about the state of the world rather than about the health of the code.
What an empty table does not say

It does not say nobody has read the site. Reading is not recorded. It does not say the catalogue is wrong, or that anyone arrived and found nothing, or that anyone arrived, was served, and left without a reason that produces a row.

It says precisely this: no one has rated, reported, disputed or requested exclusion. Recorded behaviour is not the world, and this record should not be read as a verdict on the product. It is a measurement, taken honestly, of the thing this factory currently has no evidence for.
What would change it is cheap and unglamorous: outside builders and agents doing real hunts, and then saying what they used. That is the next proof. Another mechanism is not.

data.title: The factory is learning to play its own work.
data.deck: Protocol 11 leads a new review of nine projects. The useful progress is in the game itself: a Journey, recovery, sound and art, backed by a reported production release. Elsewhere, a healthy live build can still be ahead of—or behind—the source.
data.source_reference: The project portfolio report supplied by the operator on 7 October 2026, edited for public publication. Repository and production observations are reported by that source; this publication did not independently rerun the other projects.
data.lead: The strongest change in this review is a card game that now has a coherent world around it. Protocol 11 has had the most recent work, with GPT 6.1 Sol used by the operator. Its production evidence is unusually complete; its physical acceptance is still a separate question.
data.lesson: Play the integrated product, challenge a gate when its requirement has retired, and ask the deployed origin which build it serves. A green check can support a claim; it cannot choose the claim.

children.text: Protocol 11 takes the lead

The House Circuit now gives the game a twelve-stage Journey with distinct mastery conditions and safe progress migration. Solo GO NUCLEAR has undo and restart, including the ability to roll back a bot reply. Room and cast artwork, stable theme geometry and refreshed sound make those systems feel part of the same game.

The supplied report records a settled production release matching the reviewed source, deployed asset hashes, readiness checks and live Chromium and WebKit gameplay checks. That is reported production verification, not a claim that Woodhouse has repeated the qualification. Physical iPhone play, sustained sessions and final art judgement still need their own evidence.
A strong release can sit behind newer source

SHOALSHOT is the clearest example. Its proven production build is healthy. Later first-catch Field Note work exposed recovery and browser failures, and the newer source stayed unreleased. Holding production at the qualified version is useful release discipline. The remaining question is also a design question: should automatic fire interrupt the player with a blocking discovery reveal?

Bubbles and Asset Hunter have newer source than the latest exact production receipt in the supplied report. Bubbles is resolving interaction and evidence debt. Asset Hunter has broadened from GitHub discovery to source-neutral ingestion, with a local folder, byte inspection and portable packs. Those are real implementation gains. They still need current release proof and outside use.
The rest of the portfolio has different work ahead

Fighter is turning observed battle failures into presentation changes and useful gates. LoftwahFM has a capable listener but a paused delivery lane. Pirates still needs source parity before expansion. MAX cannot turn software qualification into evidence that someone can find a real walker. Club needs renewed execution of its hospitality journey.

Each dossier now carries the 7 October report review, its source and the next proof. The older snapshots remain readable. Reviewing a supplied report is distinct from independently inspecting every repository or every live deployment.
Better judgement is the factory improvement

Across the report, the most encouraging behaviour is agents playing the products and finding defects that a ticket did not predict. A skipped ending, an unreachable catch, a battle that measures well but reads badly: the integrated experience supplies the requirement.

The response should stay small and concrete. Keep the always-on instructions short. Load detailed guidance when the work needs it. Adopt a tool at a real seam, give every process addition a failure it prevents, and retire a check when its original requirement no longer exists.

Model choice belongs to this dated account of the work. GPT 6.1 Sol is what the operator reports using for the recent Protocol 11 work; it is not a permanent rule for the factory. The durable rule is to put capable judgement at the point where it changes the outcome.

children.text: A useful hub knows who owns the work.

Woodhouse connects independent products through reviewed dossiers and evidence. LoftwahFM supplies music and station programming; the games keep control of their own player experience. A shared sound source does not require a shared game engine, visual identity or release service.

The public Radio collection now includes two dated original shows: Dead Air Department — Press Start and Smoko Circuit — Member Benefits. Their synthetic presenter scenes and catalogue music are published for replay. Autonomous refresh and full format/acting qualification remain open; these shows do not establish commercial demand or verified use in a game.

A final source check found SHOALSHOT had merged client 1.0.0 while this review was being prepared. Bubbles also records an active integration lane. The review now distinguishes those observations from the three remaining planned consumers, without promoting implementation or branch work into a production claim.

children.text: What changes the next decision

An agent can follow the upstream contract and its own game issue, select a compatible client, then record the installed version, deployment and listening evidence. New consumers enter through reviewed project identities and a capability review; no fixed five-game registry determines who may join.

Technical intelligence is useful when it changes a concrete compatibility or quality decision. Product intelligence is useful when it identifies an audience and a cheap demand test. Supplied reports remain hypotheses until checked against sources; a plausible pitch does not establish demand. Those investigations belong in their existing work, rather than another generator or recurring orchestration service.

children.text: Music that travels without flattening the games.

children.text: Let the music lead people back to the games.

Game-linked radio discovery and aggregate analytics have shipped. Visits, playback starts, audible progress and referrals answer different questions; the existence of that instrumentation does not prove an audience or justify a ranking. SHOALSHOT installs the new telemetry-capable client, while other consumers retain earlier supported versions.

Publishing original game soundtracks as proper albums remains open in FM #243. Existing recordings can use the established catalogue workflow, with game-specific covers, source provenance, shared-track associations and clearly labelled alternate versions. New content should help listeners discover the game that produced it.

Inclusive station discovery and continuous All Stations/My Mix remain open in #242 and #244. Fighter’s current station shuffle and SHOALSHOT’s manual Shuffle are real features; neither completes a shared, automatically refreshed mix of music and speech.

children.text: Give people a reason to keep listening.

Dead Air Department and Smoko Circuit are published curated shows. Their technical release is distinct from a repeatable autonomous production operation and from human judgement of acting, comedy and pacing. Topical satire, evergreen material and recurring characters should coexist, with correction, expiry, provenance, spending and fallback handled by the owning programme.
The next useful evidence is material people choose to hear again. Producing more audio, adding another provider or collecting playback events does not by itself establish entertainment value.
A playable game still has to feel good.

Protocol 11’s progress is substantial, including its playable Journey and native radio. Current player reports still identify automatic hand reordering and shifting targets, unclear layoff destinations, insufficient Flaming feedback and desktop scrolling that hides laid-down groups. The latest issues #215, #216 and #218 remain open; earlier layout repairs do not justify calling them resolved.

Interaction should support a predictable consecutive play, clear legal destinations and stable geometry on desktop and phone. Inspecting those root behaviours matters more than preserving an immature implementation or adding another cosmetic highlight.

content.context: Successful radio delivery is separate from card-play correctness.

children.text: Make the first impression and the return visit count.

The four phone games have installation-discovery work tracked. A useful install action, platform guidance and recognition of installed or dismissed state are the outcome; a PWA manifest alone does not help someone find it.

Woodhouse #19 coordinates the promotional-image reset. Each game needs imagery that makes its own experience appealing. Strong earlier poster or card-night concepts can be improved with correct branding; identical templates and technically valid metadata are insufficient creative proof.

Achievement, holographic and unlock work remains tracked across the games. Rewards should make an earned moment satisfying in the game’s own visual language, with meaningful earning conditions. This review found no completion receipts for the installation, artwork or reward programmes.

content.label: Discovery, artwork and rewards review
content.context: Existing owners remain authoritative; no parallel backlog was created.

children.text: The factory’s job is to turn this into better products.

Woodhouse now represents the shared radio relationship using the existing dossiers, dated statuses, capability review and evidence. Historical reviews remain dated, and unrelated projects are not given a fresh delivery claim. The same records serve readers and agent facts.

The useful next moves sit with their existing owners: Protocol 11 interaction correctness; FM soundtrack publishing, station mixing and entertaining programming; then discoverable installation, persuasive artwork and satisfying rewards. Reuse should make each product stronger while preserving independent identity, offline behaviour and release gates.

data.title: Reuse earns its place.
data.deck: Radio already connects independent games. Asset Hunter can package what it finds. The next useful test is whether someone chooses to listen, play or build with the result.
data.source_reference: Portfolio Brain intelligence supplied for 12 October 2026, reconciled with current source, product contracts, owning records and the public radio 1.2.0 integrity manifest. Game adoption uses the separate 11 October Woodhouse review; this publication does not claim a fresh playthrough of those games.
data.lead: The factory has two useful things to put in somebody else’s hands: music inside games, and assets with the evidence needed to use them. Neither needs a larger platform before it can be tested.
data.lesson: Choose one real experience, make it easy to try, and observe what another person does with it.

children.text: The shared capability is already audible.

LoftwahFM publishes music stations, original presenter shows and a versioned radio client. Four games have separately reviewed implementations, deployments and scoped browser receipts. Each game keeps its own audio owner, controls and release gates. Pirates remains planned. Physical-device behaviour and human listening quality still need their own acceptance.

This is a stronger reason to reuse something than similar terminology across repositories. The earlier proposal for one common browser-and-evidence framework failed the implementation comparison. Those projects solved different failures; the lessons survived without a shared package.

Give the next builder something usable.

Asset Hunter now has an implemented portable-pack path. Permitted files travel with their provenance and attribution; reference-only and review-required material stays as records. The archive can be reproduced and the recipient can verify its contents.

That gives developers and coding agents a concrete proposition: less repeated investigation between finding a useful resource and using it. The cheap next test is one recipient using one pack in a real project, followed by an unfamiliar builder. Record what worked, what needed explanation and whether the handoff saved effort. children.text: What would you use it for?

Say you want a website for your work. You need somewhere to introduce yourself, organise projects and change the content later. Or you are building workshop listings, a community directory or a client’s case-study site. Each needs its own structure and editing controls.

App Composer helps turn that requirement into work a coding agent can carry through. Get Ready prepares the environment. Init captures what you want to make. The content builder lets you design the fields people will edit. You can build a standalone application, use an existing mini-app or connect several when the connection is useful.

The browser gives you the planning and configuration tools. The build happens with your authorised agent, source repository and chosen services. Browsing Composer or exporting a specification does not start a cloud deployment.
Explore App Composer
What is Linkarooie?

Linkarooie is a creator’s home page: a profile, social links and a curated collection of the things you want people to find. Use it to bring your music, games, projects, writing and other links together at one address. A visitor can browse featured picks, move between groups or search the collection.

Loftwah’s live page shows that purpose. Music has a home, games lead straight to play, and projects and writing sit in their own groups. An invited owner can arrange cards, preview changes, publish or hide links, and change the profile’s appearance. Init also exposes profile settings such as the handle, introduction, social addresses, portrait and banner.
App Composer is the studio; Linkarooie is one of its reusable apps. Loftwah’s profile is a configured instance of that app. Another creator would bring their own identity, links and content.
Visit Loftwah’s Linkarooie profile

Here / there, the photo guestbook, adds a separate option: invited people can leave photos and messages for approval, and Linkarooie can feature approved entries. That is useful for a community or shared collection. A page of your own links can stand on its own.
The rest of the studio

Get Ready handles the work before the application: inspect the project folder, check the tools and account connections, prepare the supported starter and verify it at an HTTPS address. You handle official sign-in and decisions about access or spending. The agent handles routine technical work and reports what it actually checked.

Init is the structured brief. Choose the intended app or combination, write its title and introduction, set its appearance and describe where it should run. You can preview the configuration, save a draft on your device, download the specification and copy the matching request to your agent.

EmDash is the content management system: it supplies editing and administration for the app’s content. Cloudflare is the currently supported hosting platform. Your coding agent builds the application around those choices. Multiple mini-apps are optional: a site with one content collection can be a sensible project in its own right.

For an app with editable records, the content builder goes further. It has starting patterns for workshop listings, project case studies, a community directory and project enquiries. You can change the fields, try fictional entries and export a model or an EmDash seed. A seed is a file that defines the content structure for the CMS.
Try the content and field builder

There are useful standalone tools too. Link Check inspects a supported website URL’s icons, social images and search metadata, then exports findings you can take to your agent. Hello World is the small deployment reference for checking the setup before committing to a larger app. The app library explains what each tool does and links to its source.

How to make a start

If you are new to the workflow, open Learn. It walks through meeting the agent, preparing the environment, changing a small app, checking the live result, shaping content and maintaining what you made. You can read it before setting anything up.
Follow the tutorial

For a creator page, start with Get Ready in your chosen project folder. Give the page’s setup request to Codex. Let the agent inspect existing work and check the supported environment, then complete official account sign-in when required. The currently verified setup uses Codex on an Apple Silicon Mac with existing supported account paths; fresh-account and new-domain setup remain unfinished.
Prepare the environment with Get Ready

Next, open Init and choose Linkarooie. Set the profile text and appearance, add the links you want on the page, and describe the intended address. Download the spec and give its copied request to your agent. The demonstrated configuration path updates Loftwah’s existing app pair. A new creator’s Linkarooie deployment still needs its own implementation and live checks, even with an existing cloud account; exporting the spec does not provision it.
Configure an app in Init

For a content-led site, try the Project case studies pattern in the field builder instead. Preview the fictional example, change the model to fit your work and export it. The supplied new-project request describes an independent local EmDash site with a collection and individual entry pages. Public submission forms and cloud deployment still need their own implementation and verification.

For an existing instance, an invited owner uses its admin for everyday content and configuration. Loftwah’s Linkarooie owner can arrange and publish links there; structural changes and maintenance go to the agent. That keeps changing a link an editing task, while adding a new kind of feature remains development work.
Why connect apps at all?

Some jobs belong together without becoming the same job. A guestbook receives and moderates a photo; a creator’s page gives an approved contribution another place to appear. In the live connected example, the apps retain separate source, configuration and storage. Linkarooie checks the photo’s current publication status at the guestbook.

Hide the source and the controlled feature disappears from both public views on the next request. Already downloaded copies remain outside that control. Separate apps also mean contracts and versions to maintain. That tradeoff is worth considering when the connection improves the product.

App Composer’s broader purpose is to help you prepare, build and keep operating software you can change. Its current tools and working apps give you concrete places to start. A universal one-click customer service, completed WordPress migration and every proposed integration remain work to prove.

data.title: The same prompt, twice.
data.deck: Run a first pass to completion, then run the exact same prompt again against what it produced. On one task it found a real defect the first pass had tested and missed. On another it found nothing at all.
data.source_reference: Two sequential passes of one unchanged prompt on two bounded repository tasks, run 22 October 2026 from commit 7c0bf22 in isolated worktrees, each pass a fresh default agent session on deepseek-v4.1-flash through opencode-go (max variant). The exact prompts are printed in the article and recorded with the measurements. No private repository body, issue comment or conversation is reproduced.
data.lead: The second pass is not a review. It is the same instructions, executed again against a finished artefact, and it can be queued behind the first.
data.lesson: In one small task, a repeated pass caught and repaired a defect the first pass and its tests missed. In another it found nothing. It costs a full pass.

children.text: The observation

Dean noticed it while running work through agents here. When the same request was queued a second time after the first run had finished, the result often came back better. Not merely different. Better against the words that were originally asked for.

That is a strange thing for a system to do. The second run has no new instruction, no reviewer, no hint about what went wrong. It has the brief it already answered and the work that answering it produced.
What the technique actually is
Run the first pass to completion. Commit it. Then send the exact same prompt again, against the state it produced.

The repeat can be queued before the first pass finishes. When the first job completes, the second starts from the committed artefact; nobody has to watch for the finish and schedule it by hand. A stop gate between the passes is optional, not part of the definition.

Three things make it what it is. The passes are sequential, so the second one starts after the first has stopped. The prompt is unchanged, character for character, including its awkward bits. And the first pass has to be finished, not paused: the second pass needs a real artefact to read, not a half-built one it can carry on from.

It is not a retry after an error, which assumes the first run failed. It is not a loop, which has no reason to stop. It is not two agents reviewing each other, which needs a second set of instructions and produces a second opinion rather than a second attempt. And it is never two runs on the same working tree at the same time.
The only new input is the artefact

Published work on improving a first answer usually adds something the first run did not have. Self-Refine has the model critique its own output and revise from that critique. Reflexion turns failures into written reflections that inform later attempts. An evaluator-optimizer pair gives a second model the first model's output plus explicit criteria.

Double prompting adds neither critique nor criteria. It adds the finished artefact and the original words, and nothing else. That is the mechanism, and it is also the weakness: if the artefact looks plausible and the brief is vague, the second pass may find nothing in the new state that contradicts the first. Repeating the words does not make them unambiguous.

content.title: The same prompt, twice
content.description: A sequence diagram with three participants — operator, agent and working tree. The operator sends the task brief once. The agent runs a first pass that plans, implements and self-tests, then commits artefact A and reports the pass complete. The same brief is queued to start after pass one; an optional stop gate can interrupt the queue. The agent reads the brief against artefact A, finds omissions and defects, repairs them and adds a regression test, then reports a verified result.
content.caption: Sequential by construction. The second pass can be queued in advance; a stop gate is optional.

The same brief is queued to start after pass one. An optional stop gate can accept, stop or continue before it runs. 5. Agent runs pass two, reading the brief against artefact A. 6. Agent repairs omissions or defects and adds a regression test. 7. Operator verifies the result.
Two tasks, one prompt each

Two small repository tasks ran on 22 October 2026. Each had its own git worktree from commit 7c0bf22, and nothing else touched that worktree between passes. Each pass was a fresh default agent session on deepseek-v4.1-flash through opencode-go, max variant; model choice was not a variable. The exact prompt for each task is printed below.
The first task carried six requirements. The second carried one. The repeated pass had something to do on the first and nothing on the second.
Task one: a script with six requirements

The brief asked for a small script that reads the published dispatches from the content model and prints one line each: review date, slug, block count and word count. It named five further requirements — a JSON mode with four exact keys, a non-zero exit that names any published dispatch missing a lesson or a source reference, a test file using a temporary fixture rather than the real content, an optional path argument so the test could pass that fixture, and one new row in the operator index. Then: change nothing else.

Pass one returned all six. The script worked, the JSON keys were exact, the exit path named the right slugs, the fixture argument existed, the test file covered the shape and the failure, and the index row was there. Its three tests passed. By the ordinary test of a finished task — tests green, every named requirement visibly present — the work was done.

Pass two read the same brief against that code and found a counting bug. The word counter walked the portable-text tree and added up every string it met. Inside an object it only descended into reader-visible fields, which kept most structural noise out. Inside an array it carried no field name at all, so every element counted. Formatting marks such as bold live in arrays of bare strings. A dispatch with fourteen bold or italic runs therefore reported fourteen words that no reader would ever read.

At the time of the experiment, ten of the nineteen published dispatches carried formatting marks. Eight of them had a non-empty mark array, so eight word counts were wrong: fifty-three words too high in total, by as much as fourteen on a single dispatch. Pass two made the walk carry the owning field through arrays, added a regression test that fails when a mark is counted as a word, and left the rest alone. Two files changed.

This one was not exotic, but the first pass did not see it. The first pass was still deciding what the code should be; it tested the JSON shape and the failure path — the things the brief made explicit — and wrote its own word counter without a test that pinned down what a word was.

children.text: Task two: nothing to do

The second brief asked for one pure date function returning whole days between two ISO dates, with a range error on an invalid date, and a test covering a positive case, a zero case, a negative case and the throw. One requirement, one behaviour, one test file.

Pass one did the work in twenty-seven seconds. Pass two read the code against the brief, re-ran the tests, checked the timezone handling and the rejection of impossible dates such as 30 February, and changed nothing. It also declined to commit an empty change, which is the right call and worth stating: a second pass that produces no diff should say so, not manufacture one to look busy.
That is the honest other half. A repeated pass is not free improvement. Sometimes it is a confirmation, and a confirmation costs the same as a repair.

children.text: The tailored review prompt is reproduced in the observation record, along with the commits, timings and limitations.
Observation record for this article
A pointed review found it too

To test whether the identical prompt is doing something special, a third run audited the first pass's code in a fresh context with a tailored review prompt. It was asked to check each requirement, to answer one pointed question about formatting marks, and to report rather than repair. It found the same defect, reproduced it with a two-line fixture, and reported the real impact — in 186 seconds, with no changes to the repository.

That is not an equivalent comparison. The reviewer was told where to look, and it was told not to fix what it found. Finding the defect shows that a reviewer with the right question can identify it; it does not show that an unprompted review would, and the absence of a repair follows from the instruction. The repeated pass had no such hint, but it was asked to finish the work, which is why it left a fix and a regression test behind.

The recorded elapsed times were 186 seconds for the review and 144 seconds for the repeated pass. Those figures support no general cost advantage in either direction; this article does not claim one. A review prompt is the right instrument when you want a report. A repeated pass is the right instrument when you want the work finished.
What published work does and does not establish
Self-Refine reports

about a twenty per cent absolute average improvement across seven tasks when one model generates, critiques and revises its own output. That is iterative refinement with feedback, not repetition: the critique is new input, and it is the reason the method works.
Reflexion

goes further and stores written reflections in memory between attempts, reaching 91% pass@1 on HumanEval against the 80% reported for GPT-4 at the time. Again the improvement is attributed to the reflection, which is deliberately kept and reused.
The cautionary result is blunter. Huang and colleagues
found

that models struggle to correct their own reasoning without external feedback, and that performance sometimes degrades after self-correction. Their setting is reasoning tasks with no external signal. An artefact with tests is a kind of external signal, which may be why repetition helped here and may also be why it would not help on a task with nothing checkable in it.
Anthropic's
evaluator-optimizer
guidance names the conditions plainly: clear evaluation criteria, and iterative refinement that demonstrably adds value. Its
long-running-agent work

is closer to what this article describes. It observes that each new session begins with no memory of the last, that agents tend to attempt too much at once, and that a later agent will look around, see progress, and declare the job done. The second pass here is a fresh session with the same brief, so it inherits that failure mode as well as the benefit.

I did not find a published study of this exact procedure — one prompt, twice, no other input. Treat the numbers here as one small experiment rather than a result about models in general. The four papers and two engineering notes named above are the closest published work I found, and none of them tests this procedure.
Where it goes wrong

The documented failure mode is declaring victory. A second agent looks at a plausible artefact, sees that work has happened, and concludes the work is finished. In task two that conclusion was correct. In a task left half-done it is the most expensive mistake available, because it converts an incomplete first pass into a confident final one.

The second pass can also inherit the first pass's blind spots. Both runs share a model, a brief and now an artefact; if the brief is ambiguous in the same place for both, the ambiguity survives. The tailored review run found the same defect as the identical pass, which is reassuring for this defect and no evidence at all for the next one.

Nothing observed here produced a regression, and that is not evidence that repetitions are safe. A second pass that believes it has found a problem will change code, and a change made to satisfy an imagined requirement is a regression with a confident commit message. The mitigation is the same as for any change: the first pass must be committed and tests must exist before the second pass runs.

The cost is a full pass. Pass two on task one took 144 seconds against a first pass that was not separately timed; pass two on task two took under 24 seconds and produced nothing. The observation record does not include token or cost figures, and this article does not estimate them.
The recipe
1. Write the brief as the thing you want, including the awkward constraints. The second pass reads this text against the artefact, so anything you left out of the brief is unlikely to be recovered.
2. Let the first pass finish and commit. A second pass against uncommitted work has no clean baseline and no way to throw the second attempt away.

3. Queue the same text to run after the first pass completes. You can queue it in advance; the repeat does not need someone to watch the first job and start the second. If you want a decision point, put an optional stop gate before it runs. Existing cancellation, validation and permission boundaries still apply.
4. Send the same text again. Not a summary, not a review request, not a list of what you think is wrong. The technique is the repetition, so changing the prompt changes the experiment.
5. Require the work, not a report. Ask for the fix and a test that would have caught the defect. A second pass that only describes problems has spent a pass to become a reviewer.
6. Compare the two commits. If the second pass changed nothing, say so and stop. If it changed something, the diff is the evidence and the tests are the check.
When to stop

Task two suggests that a second pass can be wasted on a small, fully specified change. One task cannot turn that into a rule. A brief with a single requirement can still conceal substantial complexity, so judge the artefact and the uncertainty around it, not the requirement count.

Stop when the second pass changes things the brief did not ask for. Prose changes are not automatically churn: if the task is to improve the prose, that may be the work. The test is whether the diff serves the brief, whatever kind of change it is.
Stop after one repeat unless you have a specific reason for a third. This experiment says nothing about three passes, and every extra pass costs another full run.
What it means for scheduling

If this belongs in a workflow at all, it can be a dependent job queued behind pass one, with the same cancellation, validation and permission boundaries as any other job. It must be sequential. Two passes on one working tree race on the same files, and the loser's work is discarded without anyone noticing.

A stop gate is useful when someone wants to decide between the passes. It is not required: a pre-authorised repeat can start as soon as the first pass commits. Either way, the second pass is a deliberate choice made once, when the work is dispatched, not a loop.

It also counts against the same workload budget as any other job. A repeated pass is not free capacity, it is the same capacity spent twice. Whether it deserves to be automated by default is a separate question: running every task twice doubles the work to fix a problem that appeared on one of two tasks tested here.
What this does not establish

Two tasks, one repeat each. One improvement, one no-change. One comparison against a tailored review prompt that was pointed at the defect and told not to repair it. That is enough to describe a mechanism and not enough to predict a rate.

Both tasks were small repository scripts with checkable outputs and no users. Nothing here tested a feature with a design question in it, a change that touches several systems, or work where the definition of finished is contested. Those are the cases where a second pass is most likely to be confidently wrong.

Pass one of the first task was not separately timed, so the cost comparison for that task is incomplete. The observation record does not include token or cost figures, and this article does not estimate them. The model and configuration were held constant, which means this experiment says nothing about whether a different model on the second pass would do better or worse than the same prompt again.

The narrow finding is the one the evidence supports: in one small task, repeating the original prompt caught and repaired a defect that the first implementation and its tests missed. The second task found nothing. Neither result establishes a rule about requirement counts, prose changes or which approach costs less.
